title: Lady Xuanwen Giving Instruction on the Rites of Zhou
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and color on silk

image.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

source.label: CMA record: dated 1638 (Chongzhen era, wuyin year)
CMA: “fine outlines and brilliant coloring with mineral pigments”

highlight.text: Chen’s painting style is archaic in the use of fine outlines and brilliant coloring with mineral pigments. In depicting the figures, he uses the “iron-wire” brush style (fine, even lines) with deliberate control. The faces are elongated and exaggerated.

source.author: Cleveland Museum of Art
source.title: Lady Xuanwen Giving Instruction on the Rites of Zhou

source.label: CMA record: hanging scroll; ink and color on silk
CMA: “A few ritual bronzes lend the scene an antique flavor”

work.text: for the old lady, who is seated on a broad throne, is speaking to an audience of dignified scholars who seem to be submitting their writings to her. It is a motif of some [significance] represented in a form which has the solemn character of a ritual performance.
work.lead: Sirén, on this scroll (then in C. C. Wang’s collection, New York):

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V

work.text: This painting by Chen Hongshou depicts the story of Xuanwen Jun, or Lady of Literary Propagation, at a venerable age, instructing young scholars on the Confucian classics.

source.author: Cleveland Museum of Art
source.title: Lady Xuanwen Giving Instruction on the Rites of Zhou

moment.text: He was regarded as the most noted figure painter of his day in south China, as his [contemporary, Cui Zizhong], was of north China

source.author: Fang Chao-ying
source.title: Ch‘ên Hung-shou
source.publisher: in Arthur W. Hummel (ed.), Eminent Chinese of the Ch‘ing Period, vol. I, US Government Printing Office (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: I have thought that Madame Song lived during the time when the Five Barbarian Tribes were holding sway and the classics were being assigned to women. Now is the time of peace; it is rare to see women [wise enough to] uphold correctness in titles and ranks, except for my aunt.
matters.lead: Chen’s inscription, written for his aunt’s sixtieth birthday:

source.author: Chen Hongshou
source.title: Inscription on Lady Xuanwen, 1638
source.publisher: translated in the Cleveland Museum of Art collection record

matters.text: It was painted for Chen’s aunt in celebration of her 60th birthday.
